title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he spent 20 years photographing the daily life of migrant workers
dek: Others photograph the anomalies of an era; he insisted on photographing its everyday — eating, clocking in, learning English. When the 10,000-worker factory really did disappear, only a very few people had kept this archive.
why: This is not industrial analysis; it is a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography for himself and his generation. The second half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content professionals interested in the transformation of manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the factory era of the Pearl River Delta disappeared.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value unimportant
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process to make manufacturing more stable and workers more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean: anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. Although the machines had not yet replaced people, a person's value was already almost unimportant. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system that deliberately erases individual differences, record the specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like riding into a bandit's den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The carriage was already full at the Wuchang starting station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed the window with a brick and pushed people onto the train like livestock. For more than thirty hours he could not sit or drink water; after getting off, his abdomen was terribly swollen. At the Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold as a piglet’ — first they collected over twenty yuan saying it was for Dongguan, then on the highway they collected another ten yuan for the expressway fee, and if you did not pay, someone would come up and slap you, and finally you were dumped in a desolate spot with nothing around and made to change vehicles. He said he had used this term for so many years, and only last year did he understand what it meant.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 it was very hard to find work; men had a much harder time than women, and factory recruitment notices directly stated they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. By the side of National Highway 107 he saw a hiring notice. The security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people began to drop, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he remained. The captain said you are bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. After he got up, they had him spar with someone; the other man did a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg, and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: security guard at a hotel gate, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he struggled with the decision for a long time before buying his own camera: his salary was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, if you like it, then buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing, and then enlargements were another ten or twenty — in that era it was a huge expense for him. At first he photographed factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war; subconsciously he thought photography was just a matter of technique, of getting a clear shot. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he discovered there was so much learning in photography, and he had no standard by which to measure it, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson was the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: A model contest photo got tens of millions of clicks, then he was told to delete it
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding model contests; the women went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns, and uniforms they had made, and there was also pole dancing. In 2008 he changed his position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience in the distance — and sent the photos to Tencent in time; they were posted on the portal site and got tens of millions of clicks in one morning. But online comments said this was choosing a mistress for the boss, a lover for the factory director; the public opinion was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete them. Tencent said they could only hide them; other sites were spreading them virally and could not be stopped, and in the end he was given a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: That photo of a female worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
points.body: On January 5, 2011, as a senior supervisor, he entered the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. After two hours of work in the clean room there was a four-minute break; the place where they changed work clothes was hung with clean-room garments no one was wearing, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and the fellow native heard the sound and looked up at him. He said the experience others had told him when learning photography was that ‘photos where the subject looks at the lens are not good photos’, so he had long avoided using this one. Later, Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organized the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and unexpectedly it was made the lead image. Later he looked at the photo seriously and admitted it had its own appeal — different readers would have different spiritual responses, so a photographer should interpret a photo as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories had independent information, no networked computer systems, and the social security system did not require contributions, so this set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system did not recognize it — the ID number was the same, the name was the same, the household registration address was the same, and the enterprise thought you were dishonest, so they zeroed out your years of service. He said this will not do; our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those many years of service are real. When even present life is not secure, it is simply impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years from now.

points.h: Density: he photographed for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the thread of dense migrant working life, and won the Excellence Award and the Alpa Award at the third Hard Instant Image Awards. Workers' gatherings shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung with clothes, from a distance so dense no light passes through; and workshop switches, key cabinets, storage cabinets for bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures creating a visual sense of density. He said at first it was unconscious; every day he shot with his phone, he shot when organizing security training, he shot when he randomly saw a fellow worker on the road, and over time it accumulated — all told, he had shot for almost 20 years. When there were so many factories and so much of an era, he had not observed it that way; then one morning he discovered how terrifying it was — even the switches looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as warp, space as weft: using a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The complete thread he worked out was: time as warp, space as weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, and the impact of capital on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a comprehensive three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text, and physical objects. Later he changed methods: starting from the keyword ‘migrant work’, he found ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, getting 322, and went into Baidu Images and began screenshotting all of them — this is the internet's understanding of migrant work, presented together with his own understanding from actually photographing it in one huge exhibition space. He said this is how we view the era in an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compared himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers who carry the loads are all Sherpas; I will just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets being transported; later it referred to being cheated by middlemen and drivers who added charges layer by layer on the way to work.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally renowned photography agency; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers on its website one by one.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it was not like you just got on a vehicle — you felt you had gotten into a bandit's den.
This is this era: we view the era in an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.

I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we arrive at will certainly not be bad; but if we can see a society in a single day, it will certainly be very shallow.
